newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash recovery and probe may top $100 million.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash recovery and probe may top $100 million.

text.p: The cost of recovery and investigation of the TWA Flight 800 crash will probably top $100 million, National Transportation Safety Board Chairman James Hall said on Tuesday.

Hall, speaking to a group of disaster mitigation experts, said a public hearing on the TWA disaster will be held in late summer and called the investigation "the largest reconstruction effort of any accident wreckage in history."
He said the $100 million figure included local police, fire and coroner expenses as well as the cost of recovering pieces of the jetliner from the ocean and the effort to find a cause.
The Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean July 17, 1996, minutes after taking off from Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.
Hall also chided federal regulators and transportation companies for failing to move quickly enough on lifesaving safety recommendations.
"Our frustration is that often lessons from accidents are forgotten or ignored," Hall told the gathering of government disaster planners and private-sector consultants.
He cited the crash of ValueJet Flight 592, which plunged into Florida's Everglades in May 1996, killing all 110 people on board. The crash may have been caused by a fire in the DC-9's cargo hold.

Hall said his agency recommended fire detection, suppression and fighting equipment in cargo holds after a similar incident aboard a 1988 American Airlines flight to Nashville, Tennessee, in which no one was seriously injured.

"The sad fact is that ValueJet 592 had no more equipment to warn them or fight the fire than did the American Airlines flight six years earlier," Hall said. "It is nine years since the Nashville incident and crews are still without the means to fight a cargo fire and have no means for detection."
The final report on the ValueJet crash was being written by NTSB investigators and likely would be issued at the board's meeting in July, Hall said.
Hall said some transportation companies' corporate cultures did not put safety first. "Some do little to avoid, even invite disaster," he said.
